title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory audit that tested conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered thresholds; provenance timestamp heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy on a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample. The preregistered design (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) specified 150 item pairs evaluated with a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") and a deterministic NetOps verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks produced by a deterministic generator and shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false). No preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags occurred; consequently no guarded exclusions or replacements were applied. All 150 baseline and matched guarded episodes passed the verifier (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We reconcile the preregistration→execution evidence, explain why the run was degenerate for detecting generation‑level contamination (artifact‑grounded explanation: synthetic provenance + shared generation semantics), and provide artifact‑grounded recommendations—provenance‑rich sampling, independent per‑condition generation, multi‑model scope, and richer detector logging—to increase audit sensitivity in future studies.

sections.introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) are being applied to operational NetOps tasks such as intent‑to‑configuration translation and automated configuration repair. For practitioners and researchers, benchmarked success rates must reflect genuine capability rather than dataset leakage or templated items that leaked into model training corpora. Recent surveys and benchmark studies repeatedly flag two evaluation risks: contamination (benchmark items or templated prompts present in model training corpora) and construct invalidity (benchmarks that do not capture operational complexity). These risks motivate contamination‑aware audits that pair deterministic detectors with functional verifiers.

This work preregistered and executed such an audit. Our central research question asks: under a conservative set of deterministic detectors and a guarded exclusion policy, how many high‑confidence contamination flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and how much does applying those controls change an LLM's verifier pass rate? We executed the preregistered plan (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) end‑to‑end and archived the generation outputs, validator traces, transformation logs, and execution manifest. The run used a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") and a deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5).

Our contributions are: (1) a fully preregistered confirmatory experiment executed and archived under deterministic artifacts; (2) artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 with complete validator traces; and (3) a preregistration→execution reconciliation that explains why this execution produced a degenerate null for the primary estimand and provides concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations for improving audit sensitivity in future work. We bound our claims: because the executed sample used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks and shared generation semantics (recorded in the archived model_configuration and task_manifest), the observed zero‑flag outcome does not imply absence of contamination in independent public benchmarks.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluations. Prior system and benchmark efforts demonstrate that LLMs can produce useful network configuration artifacts under constrained conditions and that integrating formal verifiers or iterative validate–repair loops increases empirical reliability compared to unguided generation. Benchmarks for configuration repair and intent translation (recent arXiv and conference reports) show both promise and per‑case regressions, motivating verifier‑backed evaluation pipelines.

Contamination and evaluation validity. Methodological analyses and surveys call for contamination‑aware evaluation practice: exact‑match fingerprinting, fuzzy n‑gram overlap detectors, provenance tracing, and paraphrase‑robust detectors have all been proposed to reduce false positive performance arising from leaked training data. Our audit implements a conservative subset of these defenses (exact normalized equality, fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds, and provenance timestamp heuristics) and pairs them with a deterministic, oracle‑style verifier to operationalize the intent→configuration success criterion.

Positioning. Unlike broad capability benchmarks that report absolute scores across model families, our work is a focused, artifact‑anchored audit: we experimentally evaluate whether a particular preregistered set of contamination controls would alter verifier‑measured success on a reproducible sample under the executed semantics. The paper documents where the preregistered checks were informative and where execution choices limited sensitivity.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. We preregistered the experiment (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) before executing any model calls. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) across item×model pairs; the primary confirmatory test is an exact two‑sided McNemar test. The analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the point estimate and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI using 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729).

Detectors and guarded policy (preregistered). The detector suite consisted of: (1) exact normalized token equality after canonicalization; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap (Jaccard/overlap) with preregistered thresholds: high‑confidence flag if overlap ≥ 0.80, medium if in [0.50, 0.80); and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item source timestamps to model training cutoffs. The guarded policy deterministically excluded only high‑confidence flags (exact match OR fuzzy overlap ≥ 0.80). Excluded items were to be replaced deterministically via generator retemplating and topology augmentation subject to a fixed embedding similarity constraint; replacement semantics were codified in the preregistration transformation contract.

Sampling, generation, and critical execution semantics. The preregistration specified four candidate dataset scopes and allowed deterministic task generators for reproducibility. The executed run used deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 to produce synthetic tasks (source_identifier = "synthetic-netops:") for the confirmatory 150‑item sample. Critically, execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false): when no high‑confidence exclusions occur, a single shared model generation per item serves both baseline and guarded episodes. This setting reduced model calls used to 150 (one shared generation per item) rather than two per pair and is recorded in the archived model_configuration artifact.

Verifier and scoring. We used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the verification oracle. For intent→configuration tasks the verifier executes parse→state‑update→property checks and returns a binary pass/fail plus structured traces (parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, final_state, violation codes). The prespecified scoring rule is full_intent_constraint_validation: the generated configuration must achieve the expected final state and respect workflow constraints. Per‑episode validator traces were archived for auditing.

Planned sensitivity analyses. The preregistered analysis included sensitivity checks: (a) varying fuzzy thresholds (0.50, 0.65, 0.80); (b) treating failed model calls as failures; and (c) subgroup analyses by templated vs realistic task classifiers. We also documented power guidance in the preregistration: the originally recommended multi‑model design targeted detection of ~5 percentage‑point paired differences at 80% power. The single‑model design executed here reduces power and increases detectable effect size; these power tradeoffs are discussed below.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reconciliation. The executor completed planned_episode_count = 300 episodes (150 pairs) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, the run performed a single shared model generation per item, yielding model_calls_used = 150 rather than the preregistered maximum of 300. Deterministic_reconciliation confirms: complete_pair_count = 150, n_11 = 150, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0, and consistent provider call accounting. These exact counts are archived in the execution manifest and analysis artifacts.

Contamination detector outcomes. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags for the executed sample; analysis/contamination_summary.csv contains no flagged episodes. The detector implementation logged only episodes meeting flagging criteria or requiring replacement handling; because no high‑confidence flags occurred, the archived detector logs do not contain a distribution of per‑item fuzzy‑overlap scores for this run. Therefore, we report the artifact‑verified absence of high‑confidence flags rather than deriving or inventing per‑item overlap summaries that are not present in the archive.

Verifier outcomes and primary estimand. The deterministic verifier returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) = 0.0 percentage points. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All per‑episode validator traces and response texts are archived under execution/scoring and execution/responses; representative exemplars are included in the archived manifest.

Representative exemplar. A representative episode (pair‑000001) illustrates the artifact format and verification outcome. Reference answer and normalized model response are identical: "interface edge1 admin down\ninterface edge1 vlan 30\ninterface edge1 mtu 1600\ninterface edge1 admin up". The verifier returned score = 1 with parsed_command_count = 4 and required_command_count = 4; validator_trace records final_state and observed_touched_field_count = 3. The exemplar artifacts (response text and validator trace) are archived and linked in the execution bundle.

Absence of fuzzy‑overlap aggregates and interpretive consequences. The preregistered fuzzy‑overlap detector would have produced per‑item overlap scores and flagged items that met thresholds. In this execution the detector produced no high‑confidence flags and thus recorded no replacement events; consequently the archive lacks a per‑item overlap distribution for the sampled items. This absence is itself an execution fact recorded in the transformation and analysis artifacts and constrains interpretation: we cannot empirically say whether items would have been close to the threshold under a different detector‑logging policy or under paraphrase‑sensitive detection.
sections.discussion:
Why the run was degenerate for the primary estimand. Two archivable execution facts explain the degenerate outcome. First, the sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:"), so canonicalized exact matches to public corpus fingerprints and high fuzzy 5‑gram overlaps above the preregistered high‑confidence threshold did not arise. Second, execution used independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate): when no exclusions were triggered a single shared generation per item was reused for both baseline and guarded episodes. Both facts are explicitly recorded in the archived model_configuration.json and task_manifest.jsonl and together produced identical baseline and guarded outputs per item, mechanically preventing the paired test from observing generation‑level discordance in this run.

What this execution answers and what it does not. The artifact record supports a narrow answer: given provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and conservative deterministic detectors, no high‑confidence flags arose and applying the guarded exclusion policy (which did nothing because no flags occurred) produced no change in verifier pass rates. The result does not generalize to web‑sourced benchmarks, to paraphrase‑sensitive leakage, to independent per‑condition re‑generation semantics, or to broader multi‑model designs. We explicitly avoid extrapolating beyond the archive‑supported evidence.

Design lessons (artifact‑grounded recommendations). The preregistration→execution reconciliation implies specific audit improvements that follow directly from archived traces and counts: (1) use provenance‑rich public items (avoid synthetic provenance) to exercise fuzzy and provenance detectors; (2) set independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded episodes use independent model generations and cannot collapse to a shared output; (3) expand to multiple models and independent seeds to increase observable discordance and cross‑model contamination signals; (4) record per‑item fuzzy overlap scores irrespective of flag thresholds so auditors can report full overlap distributions; and (5) add paraphrase‑robust detectors and an adjudication path for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows from the recorded execution facts (model_calls_used = 150, completed_episode_count = 300, detector logging behavior) archived in the execution manifest and analysis artifacts.

Operational implications for NetOps evaluation. For practitioners the audit emphasizes that audit sensitivity is determined primarily by sampling provenance and generation semantics, not by verifier strength alone. Deterministic verifiers are necessary to measure functional correctness reliably, but verifier pass rates alone do not diagnose contamination unless detector logging and independent generation semantics allow divergence between baseline and guarded outputs. Audit protocols intended to assess contamination in public benchmarks should therefore combine provenance sampling, independent generation per condition, multi‑model sampling, and detailed detector logging.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation. In the reproducible 150‑pair synthetic sample we observed zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical verifier pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). The degenerate null outcome is artifact‑supported and stems from provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics; it does not imply absence of contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks. We document the preregistration→execution reconciliation, report exact confirmatory statistics (paired difference = 0.0 pp; 95% CI [0.0, 0.0]; McNemar p = 1.0), and provide explicit artifact‑grounded recommendations—provenance‑rich sampling, independent per‑condition generation, multi‑model scope, per‑item detector logging, and paraphrase‑robust detection—to increase audit sensitivity in future studies. All experiment artifacts, validator traces, analysis inputs/outputs, and execution manifests are archived in the execution bundle for verification as described in the Disclosure Statement.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini). Results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require additional detectors or human adjudication.

Passing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
